title: Environmental, Utility and Equipment Capacity Before Crop Loading

content.overview: The number of plants a room can physically hold is not the same as the number it can support. Crop density changes light distribution, transpiration, irrigation demand, dehumidification load, access and sanitation requirements.

vocabulary.definition: The planned load a system is intended and validated to support.
A limiting resource or process that constrains the overall system.
Available system capability above expected operating load.

sections.title: Biomass changes environmental load
sections.body: As crop size increases, transpiration and humidity load change. Environmental capacity should be evaluated across the crop cycle rather than from an empty room.

sections.title: Irrigation capacity includes distribution
sections.body: Available flow is not enough if emitters, pressure or drainage create uneven root-zone conditions. Delivery and drainage must match crop layout.

sections.title: Utility loading must preserve safe operation
sections.body: Electrical, water and access decisions should remain within qualified equipment and workplace controls rather than being improvised around plant count.

workedExamples: Adding another bench can raise plant count while removing service access and increasing interior humidity risk.
A pump that supplies total daily volume may still fail if peak irrigation zones exceed its practical distribution capacity.
commonMistakes: Sizing rooms from floor area alone.
Using temporary extension or plumbing arrangements as permanent capacity.
content.practicalApplication: Build a capacity worksheet for light coverage, expected moisture load, irrigation zones, drainage, access and qualified electrical/equipment limits before setting crop density.
content.summary: Crop loading should be constrained by the weakest validated environmental, utility, safety or workflow capacity—not by empty floor area.
